title: Practical 3: Introduction to population genetics, SNPs and PLINK
section: Introduction to population genetics, genetic diversity and SNPs
text:
Introduction to population genetics, genetic diversity and SNPs
Population genetics is the study of genetic differences within and between populations. It focuses on understanding how these differences arise, how they are distributed, and their role in evolutionary processes. Key areas of research include adaptation, speciation and population structure.

Genetic diversity: the foundation of evolution
Genetic diversity refers to the variation in DNA sequences among individuals in a population. It plays a critical role in:

Adaptation: high genetic diversity increases the likelihood that some individuals in a population can survive and reproduce under changing environmental conditions.
Evolutionary potential: diversity provides the raw material for natural selection, enabling populations to evolve over time.

Most of the genome is identical between individuals of the same species; only a small part differs. In humans, the DNA of two individuals is about 99.6% identical, while the remaining 0.4% (approximately 12 million base pairs, including structural variants) accounts for individual differences. In other species the proportion is different. Population genetic analyses use exactly this small, variable part of the genome. The differences can be neutral, beneficial or detrimental, depending on their context in the genome.


Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)
By number, SNPs are the most common type of genetic variation: a position in the genome where individuals differ in a single nucleotide (A, C, T or G). SNP and mutation do not mean the same:

A mutation is an event that creates a new change in the DNA. Every SNP once arose by mutation.
A SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) is a single nucleotide variant found in a population.
By convention, variants with MAF ≥ 1% are called common variants, those with MAF < 1% rare variants. The 1% threshold comes from human genetics and is not a biological boundary. Older sources call rare variants simply “mutations”, as in the figure below. Rare variants are also part of genetic variation.




A common but simplified classification by minor allele frequency: “SNP” (> 1%) and “mutation” (< 1%). More precisely: common and rare variant.


With our 92 eagles (184 genome copies), a MAF of 1% means fewer than two copies of the allele. The 1% threshold therefore also depends on sample size.

Key characteristics of SNPs

Frequency: by number, SNPs are the most common variants (a human genome differs from the reference at about 4–5 million sites, mostly SNPs). Structural variants (deletions, insertions, duplications) are fewer, but together they cover more base pairs.
Distribution: in humans they occur approximately every 300 to 1000 base pairs. The density depends on the species and the genomic region.
Binarity: SNPs are typically biallelic, meaning there are two possible nucleotides at a given position.



Allele types at SNP loci

Major allele: the allele with the higher frequency in the population.
Minor allele: the allele with the lower frequency. Its frequency is the MAF (minor allele frequency).

For a biallelic SNP, the major allele has a frequency above 50% and the minor allele below 50%. At multiallelic sites this is not necessarily true, which is why we keep only biallelic SNPs from the VCF (Steps of SNP analysis).
In VCF files we meet another naming: the reference allele (REF) is the one in the reference genome, the alternative allele (ALT) is the other one. The reference allele is not necessarily the major allele.
A diploid individual has one of three genotypes at each SNP:



Genotype
VCF code
Meaning




homozygous for the reference allele
0/0
e.g. A/A


heterozygous
0/1
A/G


homozygous for the alternative allele
1/1
G/G


missing genotype
./.
not enough reads at this position



Changes between two purines (A ↔︎ G) or two pyrimidines (C ↔︎ T) are transitions (Ts), all others are transversions (Tv). Transitions are more common in genomes, so the Ts/Tv ratio is a good indicator of variant calling quality (around 2–3 genome-wide in vertebrates).


SNPs in coding and non-coding regions
SNPs can occur in both non-coding and coding regions:

Non-coding regions: SNPs in these regions can affect gene regulation, splicing or the stability of RNA.
Coding regions: SNPs in these regions may be

synonymous: no change in the amino acid sequence due to redundancy in the genetic code,
nonsynonymous: a change in the amino acid sequence, potentially affecting the structure and function of the protein.





Types of single nucleotide changes.




SNPs as tools in research
Due to their abundance and ease of genotyping, SNPs have become the primary markers in association studies, which examine how genetic variations are linked to traits such as:

diseases: identifying genetic risk factors for conditions like diabetes or cancer,
phenotypes: understanding the genetic basis of traits like height, skin colour or metabolic differences.



The importance of studying SNPs
SNPs are invaluable for population genetics and genomics because they:

trace ancestry and population history: SNP patterns reveal migration, admixture and evolutionary history,
aid conservation biology: assess genetic diversity in endangered species to guide conservation efforts,
facilitate personalised medicine: help identify genetic variants associated with drug responses and diseases.

By exploring genetic diversity and SNPs, population genetics provides a powerful framework for understanding evolution, human health and biodiversity.

title: Practical 3: Introduction to population genetics, SNPs and PLINK
text:
Steps of SNP analysis
The diagram shows the steps from sequencing reads to the final merged and filtered VCF file. After basic QC and the relatedness check the pipeline splits into a dataset without LD pruning and a dataset after LD pruning, because different analyses need different datasets.






Slika 9.1: From sample to SNP dataset. In this practical we start in column 3: basic QC and relatedness; then the path splits into a dataset without and with LD pruning. Click the image to enlarge it.



Open the diagram in full size (a vector image you can zoom freely).
From now on we will work in PLINK to do some analyses and prepare the data for R.






NasvetLinux



Large analyses are usually run on Linux servers (HPC), where PLINK is called directly from the terminal. PLINK also runs on Windows and macOS, so we will run it from R. The commands are the same. If you don’t know Linux, have a look at the basic Linux commands and Tools for bioinformatics: Linux (in Slovenian).



Biallelic variants in VCF files for PLINK
When preparing VCF (Variant Call Format) files for PLINK analysis, it’s crucial to understand and focus on biallelic variants.

What are biallelic variants?
Biallelic variants are genetic variations where only two alleles are observed at a specific locus (position) in a population. In the context of SNPs, this means there are only two possible nucleotides at a given position.


Why biallelic variants for PLINK?

Simplicity: PLINK is designed to work primarily with biallelic variants, as they are easier to analyse statistically (the PLINK 1 format cannot store others at all).
Common in SNPs: most SNPs are naturally biallelic, making them ideal for population genetics studies.
Computational efficiency: biallelic variants require fewer computational resources to process and analyse.



Preparing VCF files for PLINK

Filter for biallelic sites: remove any multiallelic variants (sites with more than two alleles) from your VCF file.
Check the REF and ALT columns: the REF column should contain one allele and the ALT column only one alternative allele.
Example: a valid biallelic entry looks like chr1 100 . A G . PASS ., where A is the reference and G the single alternative allele.



Important considerations

Quality control: make sure your variants pass appropriate quality filters before including them in your PLINK analysis.
Indels: while PLINK can handle biallelic insertions and deletions (indels), some analyses are more straightforward with SNPs only.
Documentation: always document any filtering steps you perform on your VCF file before the PLINK analysis.

By focusing on biallelic variants, you ensure compatibility with PLINK and set a solid foundation for your population genetics analyses.

Some analyses are only available in PLINK 1.9 (e.g. MDS with --cluster --mds-plot and ROH with --homozyg), so install both versions. You will see for yourself when to use which: the PLINK 2 documentation says to use PLINK 1.9 for every command that is not implemented yet.

Unzip the download and save the program (only the .exe or executable file) in the data folder (see Data: white-tailed eagle). On macOS and Linux make it executable with chmod +x plink plink2.






NasvetAdvanced: PLINK in Docker (optional)





Instead of downloading the program into the data folder, you can run it in a Docker container. The advantage is that everyone uses exactly the same version of the program regardless of the operating system, and we record the version in the methods and README. This is one of the foundations of reproducibility. Docker must be installed and running (see Tools for bioinformatics: Docker, in Slovenian).
We use ready-made images from the BioContainers project:



Program
Image




PLINK 1.9
quay.io/biocontainers/plink:1.90b7.7--h18e278d_1


PLINK 2
quay.io/biocontainers/plink2:2.0.0a.6.9--h9948957_0



The label after the colon (tag) is the program version. Don’t use the latest tag, because it changes over time.
From a terminal (WSL, macOS, Linux), in the practical3 folder:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/data -w /data quay.io/biocontainers/plink2:2.0.0a.6.9--h9948957_0 plink2 --version

--rm: the container is deleted when it finishes,
-v "$PWD":/data: links the current folder to the folder /data in the container (otherwise PLINK can’t see our files),
-w /data: the working directory in the container.

In Git Bash on Windows, put MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 in front of the command, otherwise Git Bash converts the path /data into a Windows path.
From R we write a function similar to plink2():

images <- c(plink2 = "quay.io/biocontainers/plink2:2.0.0a.6.9--h9948957_0",
            plink  = "quay.io/biocontainers/plink:1.90b7.7--h18e278d_1")

plink_docker <- function(program, ...) {
  args <- c("run", "--rm", "-v", paste0(getwd(), ":/data"), "-w", "/data", images[[program]], program,
            ..., "--chr-set", "26", "no-x", "no-y", "no-xy", "no-mt")
  windows <- .Platform$OS.type == "windows"
  system2("docker", shQuote(args, type = if (windows) "cmd" else "sh"))
}

plink_docker("plink2", "--bfile", r("eagle_0"), "--freq", "--out", r("freq_docker"))

File paths must be relative (results/...), because the container only sees the practical3 folder (as /data). PLINK in the container is the Linux version, also on Windows and macOS.









OpozoriloWarning: PLINK was made for humans and SNP chips



PLINK was developed for association studies in humans (GWAS; Purcell et al. 2007). The data were genotypes from SNP chips (SNP arrays): a few hundred thousand common SNPs, chosen in advance, spread across the genome, with reliable genotypes. This leads to several assumptions that do not hold for non-model species and sequencing data (WGS, RAD):

Chromosomes. By default PLINK knows the human chromosomes 1–22, X, Y, XY and MT. For the eagle we therefore need --chr-set and --allow-extra-chr (see The plink2() function).
Hard calls only. PLINK reads only GT (0/0, 0/1, 1/1). It discards depth (DP), quality (GQ) and genotype likelihoods (PL, GL). With low coverage and ancient DNA, exactly this information is needed to tell a true heterozygote from an error.
Variable sites only. The .bim contains only SNPs, no invariant sites. Therefore π per base pair, Tajima’s D and the SFS from PLINK are not correct (Practical 4).
Default parameter values are tuned to human chips (e.g. for --homozyg and --indep-pairwise).


Example: ROH without a SNP chip
ROH (runs of homozygosity) are long segments without heterozygotes, inherited from a common ancestor of both parents. --homozyg in PLINK 1.9 searches for ROH with a sliding window (by default 50 SNPs, 1 heterozygote and 5 missing genotypes allowed per window, a ROH must have at least 100 SNPs and 1000 kb). These values suit chips with an even SNP density. With sequencing data, information is lost in several ways:

Genotype errors break ROH. WGS has many more SNPs than a chip, so a 1 Mb ROH also contains more false heterozygotes (sequencing errors, ancient DNA damage). PLINK does not know which genotype is uncertain, so it cuts a long ROH into short ones or misses it. FROH is underestimated.
Low coverage hides heterozygotes. At 2–5× coverage we often read only one allele (allelic dropout) and a heterozygote becomes a false homozygote. There are too many ROH and they are too long. Without PL/GL this cannot be corrected.
LD pruning removes SNPs. Our VCF is already pruned, so the gaps between SNPs are larger and short ROH (old inbreeding) are lost. In practice we use all SNPs for ROH.
Uneven density. With sequencing, SNPs are dense in variable regions and sparse elsewhere. The same thresholds (SNPs per window, kb per SNP) therefore do not mean equally long segments everywhere. Parameters must be adapted to the data (Meyermans et al. 2020).



Alternatives

PLINK

NgsRelate
genotype likelihoods at low coverage

–

--homozyg (PLINK 1.9)
bcftools roh, RZooRoH, ROHan, detectRUNS (R)
HMM with allele frequencies and genotype likelihoods; ROHan for low coverage and ancient DNA



So why PLINK? It is very fast (millions of SNPs in a few seconds), almost all programs read its formats, and we can compare results with many published studies. In the practicals we use it for speed. Our data are WGS filtered with DP ≥ 8 and GQ ≥ 20, so the genotypes are reliable enough as hard calls. In your own project, always check whether PLINK suits your data and justify the parameters you use.

PLINK from R
In the previous practicals we learned about R, RStudio and Quarto. R can run command-line programs with the system() function:

system("data/plink2.exe --version")

If plink2.exe is stored somewhere else than the data, we have to type the full path every time, which is not very clear:

system("C:/Users/name/Documents/EPG/data/plink2.exe --bfile results/eagle_0 --freq --out results/freq")

Instead, we write our own function with function(). The simplest version takes the arguments and puts the path to PLINK in front of them:

runPLINK <- function(PLINKoptions = "") system(paste("data/plink2.exe", PLINKoptions))
runPLINK("--bfile results/eagle_0 --freq --out results/freq")

The function appears in the Environment pane. In the practicals we use a slightly improved version plink2() (The plink2() function), which prints the command, adds the settings for the eagle chromosomes, checks for errors and shows the most important lines of the log (.log).

title: Practical 3: Introduction to population genetics, SNPs and PLINK
text:
Data: white-tailed eagle
We use data from Hansen et al. (2023), Molecular Ecology: whole genomes (WGS) of 92 white-tailed eagles from Iceland (IS), Greenland (GL), Norway (NO), Denmark (DK), Estonia (ES) and one sample from Turkey (TU). Some samples are contemporary (Con, after 1990) and some historical (His, museum specimens from ~1880–1950).






OpozoriloWatch out: property of the data



The eagle VCF is already filtered and LD-pruned (r² > 0.5). The authors uploaded only the final dataset to Dryad, so:

we cannot repeat some filters (depth, genotype quality) from scratch, but we can check them,
the dataset contains only variable sites, and some linked SNPs have already been removed. This matters for π, SFS and ROH (Practicals 4 and 6).

Variants were called with GraphTyper2 on the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) reference genome.



Folders and paths
Download E3_practical3_data.zip (100 MB) from GitHub and unzip it. You get the folder practical3 with this .qmd file, the images and the folder data. Add plink.exe and plink2.exe to the data folder and open E3_plink_EN.qmd in RStudio. The structure must be:
practical3/
├── E3_plink_EN.qmd
├── images/                   # figures
├── data/
│   ├── eagle.vcf.gz          # genotypes (VCF, compressed)
│   ├── eagle_metadata.csv    # one individual per line
│   ├── chromosoms_eagle.csv  # chromosome names
│   ├── plink.exe             # PLINK 1.9 (macOS/Linux: plink)
│   └── plink2.exe            # PLINK 2 (macOS/Linux: plink2)
└── results/                  # PLINK writes here (created automatically)
We set all paths once, at the beginning.

library(tidyverse)

data_dir    <- "data"      # folder with the data and both PLINK versions
results_dir <- "results"   # PLINK writes its files here


dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
exe <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") ".exe" else ""
plink2_path  <- normalizePath(file.path(data_dir, paste0("plink2", exe)))   # PLINK 2
plink19_path <- normalizePath(file.path(data_dir, paste0("plink", exe)))    # PLINK 1.9
vcf_path    <- file.path(data_dir, "eagle.vcf.gz")







NasvetOn your computer



In R we always use forward slashes (/), also on Windows. Don’t upload the results folder to GitHub (add it to .gitignore).




Group colours
We will use the same country colours in all practicals: islands in blue and green, mainland in warm colours.

country_colours <- c(IS = "#0072B2", GL = "#009E73",                 # islands: Iceland, Greenland
                     NO = "#D55E00", DK = "#E69F00", ES = "#CC79A7", # mainland: Norway, Denmark, Estonia
                     TU = "#7F7F7F")                                  # Turkey (1 historical sample)
period_shapes <- c(contemporary = 16, historical = 17)



Metadata
The metadata table has some columns in Slovenian; we add English versions.

meta <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "eagle_metadata.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(period = if_else(Time == "Con", "contemporary", "historical"),
         region = recode(otok_celina, otok = "island", celina = "mainland", referenca = "reference"),
         group  = skupina)

meta |>
  count(CO, region, period) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Number of individuals per country and period.")

OpombaQuestion



Which groups have very few individuals? Can we reliably estimate allele frequencies for them?




The VCF file
A VCF is a text file with two parts: the header (lines starting with ##) describes the content, followed by a table with one line per variant. The uncompressed file is 588 MB, so we don’t open it completely, we only read the beginning.

vcf_start <- readLines(gzfile(vcf_path), n = 300)   # the header has about 220 lines

header <- vcf_start[startsWith(vcf_start, "##")]
length(header)                       # number of header lines

[1] 221

grep("##FORMAT", header, value = TRUE)

OpombaQuestion



An individual has AD = 14,0 and GT = 0/0. Is this a reliable genotype? What about AD = 2,1 and GT = 0/1? Why did the authors remove genotypes with DP < 8 and GQ < 20?




The plink2() function
The function builds the command, prints it, runs it and shows the most important lines of the log (.log). It also adds --chr-set 26 no-x no-y no-xy no-mt, because the eagle has 26 autosomes. Without it, PLINK would treat chromosomes 23–26 as human X, Y, XY and MT. The function plink19() does the same with PLINK 1.9 (PLINK 1.9 also knows --chr-set).

plink2 <- function(..., show = TRUE, path = plink2_path) {
  args <- c(..., "--chr-set", "26", "no-x", "no-y", "no-xy", "no-mt", "--silent")
  out <- args[which(args == "--out") + 1]
  cat(sub("\\.exe$", "", basename(path)), c(...), "\n")

  # quotes around paths, so that folders with spaces also work
  windows <- .Platform$OS.type == "windows"
  command <- if (windows) path else shQuote(path)   # Windows adds quotes itself
  status <- system2(command, args = shQuote(args, type = if (windows) "cmd" else "sh"))

  log <- readLines(paste0(out, ".log"))
  if (status != 0) {
    cat(log, sep = "\n")
    stop("PLINK stopped with an error (see the log above).")
  }
  if (show) {
    cat(grep("loaded|remaining|removed|written|scanned", log, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
  }
  invisible(log)
}

# the same with PLINK 1.9 (e.g. --homozyg for ROH)
plink19 <- function(..., show = TRUE) plink2(..., show = show, path = plink19_path)

From the VCF we keep only biallelic SNPs (--snps-only just-acgt, --max-alleles 2), as described above. Each variant gets the ID chromosome:position (--set-all-var-ids @:#). Chromosome names in the VCF (LR606181.1) are not numbers, so we need --allow-extra-chr.

       "--snps-only", "just-acgt",
       "--max-alleles", "2",
       "--set-all-var-ids", "@:#",
       "--make-bed",
       "--out", r("eagle_0"))

With PLINK filters we remove individuals and SNPs of poor quality. For each filter we first look at the distribution, then choose a threshold and justify it. Overview of the filters:

The values in the column Frac._missing_SNPs range from 0 to 945, so we divided them by 1000. In which unit are they recorded? Do the points lie on the diagonal? What would it mean if an individual were far from it (e.g. swapped sample names)? Why is it important to always check metadata against the data?




Choosing the --mind threshold

Ancient DNA: what happens to the DNA molecule after death
Ancient DNA (aDNA) is not defined by the age of the sample but by its condition: it is any DNA from a non-living source that shows signs of degradation. Our museum eagles, about 100 years old, therefore also count as ancient DNA. After an organism dies, DNA repair stops and the molecule starts to decay (Slika 9.5):

Depurination: a purine base (A or G) is lost from the strand by hydrolysis. The sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact, but there is no base at that position (abasic site).
Nicks: the backbone is unstable at an abasic site and breaks there. A nick breaks only one strand of the double-stranded molecule.
Fragmentation: when nicks on opposite strands are close together, the molecule falls apart. Because the nicks are not exactly opposite each other, short single-stranded overhangs remain at the ends. Ancient DNA is therefore short: in the samples described by SPAAM it is on average about 30 to 50 bp long. Length depends more on the conditions in which the sample was kept than on its age, so fragments can be longer in well-preserved and younger samples.
Cytosine deamination: cytosine loses its amino group and becomes uracil (Slika 9.6). In double-stranded DNA cytosine is protected by pairing with guanine; in single-stranded DNA it is exposed, so deamination there is more than 100 times faster (Lindahl & Nyberg 1974; Frederico et al. 1993, as summarised by SPAAM). Single-stranded overhangs are at the ends of fragments, so damage accumulates at the fragment ends.







Slika 9.5: DNA degradation after death: (A) intact double-stranded DNA, (B) depurination, (C) nicks at abasic sites, (D) fragmentation into short fragments with single-stranded overhangs, (E) cytosine deamination to uracil (U, grey) in the overhangs. Source: Introduction to Ancient Metagenomics, chapter Introduction to ancient DNA (Fellows Yates et al. 2025, SPAAM); figure by Christina Warinner, CC BY-SA 4.0.



Deamination of cytosine produces uracil, which does not normally occur in DNA. Deamination of 5-methylcytosine (methylated cytosine, in vertebrates mainly at CpG sites) produces thymine directly, which is a normal DNA base. This matters when removing damage: USER enzymes remove uracil, but not thymine derived from 5-methylcytosine (below).






Slika 9.6: Deamination of cytosine to uracil (top) and of 5-methylcytosine to thymine (bottom). Source: Introduction to Ancient Metagenomics (SPAAM); figure by Christina Warinner, CC BY-SA 4.0.




How damage becomes errors in the sequence
Uracil pairs with adenine, so during amplification the polymerase incorporates A opposite uracil (instead of the G that would pair with cytosine). The new strand therefore carries A instead of G (Slika 9.7 A, “G → A misincorporation”), and in the next copy a T stands opposite this A. At a position where the living eagle had a cytosine, we therefore read C → T. The same damage read from the opposite strand appears as G → A.
The error is thus a difference from the original DNA before damage. In the data we see it as a difference from the reference genome, so it cannot be told apart from a true SNP if we look at a single site in a single individual.
The polymerase also stops at a strand break and often adds an adenine to the end (Slika 9.7 B). If this partial product anneals to another molecule in the next round of amplification, this A becomes a misincorporated nucleotide.






Slika 9.7: How ancient DNA damage becomes sequence errors. (A) Uracil (C → U) in the template causes misincorporation of A instead of G. (B) The polymerase stops at a strand break and adds an A; when this partial product anneals to another template in the next cycle, the A becomes a misincorporated nucleotide. Source: Hofreiter et al. (2001), Nucleic Acids Research 29: 4793–4799.





How we detect damage on the reads
Because damage is concentrated at fragment ends, in authentic ancient DNA the proportion of C → T and G → A substitutions is not constant along the read. Programs such as mapDamage (Jónsson et al. 2013) and DamageProfiler (Neukamm et al. 2021) calculate, for each position in the aligned reads, the proportion of reference cytosines read as T (and of reference guanines read as A). The result is a damage profile (Slika 9.8).
How to read the figure:

the x axis is the position of the nucleotide in the read: on the left from the 5′ end towards the middle, on the right from the middle towards the 3′ end,
the y axis is the proportion of substitutions at that position,
the red curve is C → T, the blue curve G → A,
in a double-stranded ancient DNA library we expect most C → T at the 5′ end and most G → A at the 3′ end; the proportion decreases towards the inside of the read.

The six panels do not show six different DNA ages; they show different profiles resulting from library preparation and technical circumstances:








Panel
What we see
Explanation




A
flat lines close to 0
modern DNA, or ancient DNA treated with USER enzymes (uracil removed)


B
jagged curves without a clear pattern
too few reads (or fragments shorter than 30 bp included): the profile cannot be assessed


C
the typical pattern at the ends, but the middle is also elevated
an elevated baseline of substitutions: reads were aligned to a wrong (too distant) reference genome, so differences from the reference are not only damage


D
high C → T at 5′, G → A at 3′, close to 0 in the middle
authentic ancient DNA, double-stranded library


E
a peak only at the last nucleotide at each end
partial USER treatment (partial UDG): damage removed everywhere except the terminal nucleotides


F
C → T at both ends, no G → A
single-stranded library: the strands are read separately, so damage appears as C → T at both ends









Slika 9.8: Damage profiles on reads (red C → T, blue G → A, by position from the 5′ to the 3′ end of the read): (A) modern DNA or a USER-treated library, (B) too few reads, (C) wrong reference (elevated baseline), (D) authentic ancient DNA, double-stranded library, (E) partial USER treatment (damage remains only on the terminal nucleotide), (F) single-stranded library. The panels do not represent different DNA ages. Source: Introduction to Ancient Metagenomics (SPAAM); adapted from nf-core/eager (Z. Fagernäs), CC BY 4.0.



A reliable profile needs enough aligned reads. SPAAM gives more than about 1000 aligned sequences as a guide; this is not a strict threshold, but a warning that with fewer reads the profile is noisy (panel B) and more sequencing is needed.
A typical profile (panel D) supports the authenticity of ancient DNA: it indicates that the DNA is not modern contamination. On its own, however, it does not prove age, and it is always interpreted together with fragment length, library preparation (double- or single-stranded, USER), number of reads and choice of reference. Damage is also not a clock: it depends more on the temperature and humidity in which the sample was kept than on its age.


Consequences for genotypes and population genetics
There are three consequences for population genetics:

false transitions (C → T, G → A), which can be mistaken for true SNPs,
more missing data, because fragments are short, coverage is lower and more sites fail quality filters,
genotype errors in both directions: at a true homozygote, damaged reads can produce a false heterozygote; at a true heterozygote, low coverage often means only one allele is read (allelic dropout), giving a false homozygote. Which error dominates depends on coverage, damage and the genotype caller.

Damage is reduced in the laboratory or bioinformatically:

USER enzymes (uracil-specific excision reagent) remove uracil (Briggs et al. 2010); partial treatment keeps damage on the terminal nucleotides so that authenticity can still be checked (Rohland et al. 2015); USER does not remove thymine derived from 5-methylcytosine,
trimming the read ends, where damage is concentrated,
taking damage into account in genotype calling (e.g. Kousathanas et al. 2017 for heterozygosity in ancient and low-coverage genomes),
using transversions only, which are not affected by cytosine deamination. This reduces the effect of damage but does not remove all errors (e.g. errors due to low coverage or alignment), and it discards most SNPs, because transitions are more common.







PomembnoTwo levels: reads and genotypes




Authenticity and quality of ancient DNA are assessed at the level of reads: fragment length, damage profile (mapDamage, DamageProfiler).
Population genetic statistics (Ts/Tv, heterozygosity, F, FST) are calculated from called genotypes.

We only have the final VCF, so we cannot see the reads. Hansen et al. (2023) report that damage was restricted to about 5 bp at the read ends and had only a minor potential effect on heterozygosity. Below we check what the genotypes can tell us.





Ancient DNA in our dataset: Ts/Tv and heterozygosity
From the .scount table we have two measures for each individual:

Ts/Tv: the ratio of transitions to transversions among the individual’s non-reference genotypes (relative to the reference genome). If many false C → T and G → A transitions remained in the data, we would expect a higher Ts/Tv in historical samples.
Heterozygosity (het): the proportion of heterozygous genotypes among called genotypes at SNPs, HET_SNP_CT / (HOM_REF_CT + HOM_ALT_SNP_CT + HET_SNP_CT). Missing genotypes are not in the denominator. This is not genome-wide heterozygosity (per base pair): the VCF contains only variable, filtered and LD-pruned sites, so the value is only useful for comparing individuals within this dataset.


samples |>
  select(vcf_id, CO, period, f_miss, `Ts/Tv` = ts_tv, `Heterozygosity at SNPs` = het) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Ts/Tv`, `Heterozygosity at SNPs`), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = factor(measure, levels = c("Ts/Tv", "Heterozygosity at SNPs")),
         period = factor(period, levels = c("historical", "contemporary"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(period, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = CO), width = 0.15, size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colours) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "Country") +
  theme_minimal()







Slika 9.9: Ts/Tv (left) and observed heterozygosity at SNPs (right) per individual, by period. Colour is country.






samples |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(n = n(), `Ts/Tv` = mean(ts_tv), heterozygosity = mean(het)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Means per period.")

The contemporary samples include 25 Icelandic eagles with very low heterozygosity, whereas the historical samples are dominated by Norwegian and Danish eagles. Within each country the two periods are mostly similar. The difference between the two period means is therefore largely a consequence of different sample composition, not necessarily of a change in diversity over time.






OpozoriloWe do not interpret the difference in means as a loss of diversity



The higher mean heterozygosity of historical samples does not prove that the population was more diverse 100 years ago. The difference can result from different representation of countries, true biological differences, differences in coverage and quality, genotype-calling errors, or which sites could be called at all. We therefore compare periods within the same country. We do not run a statistical test here: the groups are small (e.g. 2 historical Icelandic eagles), and individuals are not independent of country.



Heterozygosity and missing data

ggplot(samples, aes(f_miss, het, colour = CO, shape = period)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colours) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = period_shapes) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of missing genotypes", y = "Heterozygosity at SNPs", colour = "Country", shape = "Period") +
  theme_minimal()







Slika 9.11: Observed heterozygosity at SNPs against the proportion of missing genotypes. Each point is one individual.





Heterozygosity is calculated from called genotypes only, so for an individual with 70% missing genotypes it is based on about three times fewer sites than for an individual with no missing data. More missing data does not necessarily mean lower heterozygosity, but the estimates are not equally reliable. Missing data are also not random: at low coverage a homozygote is easier to call than a heterozygote, and quality filters may remove different sites in historical than in contemporary samples. An association between the two axes in this plot therefore does not mean that missing data cause higher or lower heterozygosity.

In historical samples, every result can be a mixture of biology and technique (less data, damage, genotyping errors). In practice, damage is checked already on the reads (e.g. mapDamage) and removed before variant calling. Another option is to use transversions only, which are not affected by deamination. Duplicated samples and close relatives (KING)
Related individuals in a sample cause problems: they inflate allele frequencies of the family, and in structure analyses (PCA, ADMIXTURE) they can create false clusters. Duplicated samples (the same individual twice) are an error that we must remove already during quality control. In QC we therefore only check relatedness: we look for duplicated samples and close relatives. A detailed analysis of relatedness (heatmaps, degrees of relationship, relatedness in small populations, ROH) follows in Practical 6.
PLINK 2 computes relatedness with the KING-robust estimator (Manichaikul et al. 2010), which does not need allele frequencies. KING coefficients are scaled so that duplicated samples have kinship 0.5, not 1. First-degree relatives (parent–offspring, siblings) have ~0.25. For duplicated samples we use the threshold 0.354 (geometric mean of 0.5 and 0.25), for first-degree relatives 0.177.

Allele frequencies (MAF)
MAF (minor allele frequency) is the frequency of the less common allele at a SNP. Rare alleles (MAF < 1–5%) are often sequencing errors, but they also carry information about recent mutations and demography. We therefore apply the MAF filter depending on the analysis:

PCA, DAPC, ADMIXTURE: rare alleles are usually removed (--maf 0.05), because they contribute little to structure but add noise,
π, SFS, ROH: no MAF filter, because it would distort the frequency distribution and underestimate diversity.

Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)
In an ideal population (random mating, no selection, migration or mutation, large population), genotype frequencies are \(p^2\), \(2pq\) and \(q^2\). Deviations from HWE can be technical (genotyping errors, paralogs that create too many heterozygotes) or biological (inbreeding, selection, population structure).

Wahlund effect
If we pool several populations with different allele frequencies, we observe a deficit of heterozygotes, even if each population is in equilibrium. This is called the Wahlund effect (we met it in a simulation in Practical 2). We test it by calculating HWE separately for two contemporary populations. The HWE test only makes sense for SNPs that are polymorphic in the group, so we exclude monomorphic ones.

OpombaQuestion



Why are there many more deviations from HWE when we pool all eagles? What would happen if we applied --hwe 1e-6 to all individuals together? Which SNPs would we remove? (Hint: exactly those that differ most between populations.)


Therefore we do not apply the HWE filter to pooled data. In practice it is applied within populations, removing only SNPs that deviate in several populations at once (which indicates a technical error, e.g. a paralog).
PLINK 2 has the option keep-fewhet for this (--hwe 1e-6 keep-fewhet): it removes only SNPs with too many heterozygotes (typical of paralogs) and keeps SNPs with a deficit of heterozygotes (typical of population structure and the Wahlund effect). The HWE filter is therefore not an automatic part of QC: we first calculate HWE and interpret the result, and apply the filter only if we can justify it.

Linkage disequilibrium (LD)
SNPs that lie close together are inherited together and carry similar information (linkage disequilibrium, LD). For PCA and ADMIXTURE, which assume independent SNPs, we therefore remove one SNP from each pair with high r² (LD pruning).
The command --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 scans windows of 50 SNPs, shifts the window by 5 SNPs and removes one SNP from each pair with r² > 0.2.

OpozoriloWatch out: property of the data (LD)



Our VCF is already pruned at r² 0.5. Additional pruning at r² 0.2 would remove many more SNPs, partly because r² is calculated over all populations together (population structure itself increases LD). Therefore we don’t apply it and keep the authors’ dataset. For analyses that need all SNPs (ROH, LD decay, π in windows), an unpruned dataset would be used in practice.



Think: where does LD pruning matter?
The diagram (Slika 9.1) splits after basic QC and relatedness into two datasets: without LD pruning and after LD pruning. Our data are only on the right branch. Before using them in Practicals 4–6, think about where this will affect the results.






OpombaQuestion: fill in the table



For each analysis, state whether LD pruning (1) has no effect, (2) affects precision or p-values, (3) biases the estimate or (4) makes the analysis impossible. Justify your answer in one sentence.

These questions can help:

Does the method assume that SNPs are independent? What happens if the same information is counted several times?
Does the method look at individual SNPs or at runs of neighbouring SNPs (windows, segments)?
Does the estimate change, or only its confidence interval?
Does pruning remove SNPs randomly with respect to allele frequency? (Hint: in a pair with high r², the SNP with the higher MAF is often kept.)







OpombaQuestion: F-statistics



Hansen et al. (2023) calculated FST on the pruned dataset. Would the global FST between Iceland and Norway change much if all SNPs were used? What about with --maf 0.05? Why does it matter for FIS and FH (plink --het) from which individuals the allele frequencies are calculated? (Hint: Wahlund effect in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE).)





All in one command
Several filters can be applied in a single command. PLINK applies them in a fixed order (individuals first, then SNPs), so we have to keep track ourselves of which filters were used:
./plink2.exe --bfile eagle_0 --mind 0.05 --geno 0.05 --maf 0.05 --make-bed --out eagle_filters
./plink2.exe --bfile eagle_filters --indep-pairwise 50 5 0.2 --out eagle_ld
./plink2.exe --bfile eagle_filters --extract eagle_ld.prune.in --make-bed --out eagle_ld_pruned

We left out --hwe, because we don’t apply it to pooled populations (Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE)).
--indep-pairwise does not remove SNPs, it only writes a list (.prune.in, .prune.out). They are removed only with --extract.

In this practical we filtered step by step, because this shows how many individuals and SNPs we lose with each filter (Filtering cascade and final dataset).






NasvetParameters from the literature



We don’t invent thresholds. We look them up in papers with similar data and cite them. The authors of the eagle paper used: QUAL ≥ 1000, GQ ≥ 20, DP ≥ 8, autosomes only, at most 25% missing genotypes per SNP, MQ ≥ 30, LD pruning r² 0.5 (window 134). Common PLINK QC values for animals are --geno 0.1–0.2, --mind 0.1–0.2 (much more lenient for ancient DNA), --maf 0.01–0.05, --hwe 1e-6 within populations. All chosen thresholds are reported in the methods.

title: Practical 3: Introduction to population genetics, SNPs and PLINK
text:
Filtering cascade and final dataset
Finally we make a table: how many SNPs and individuals are left after each step. Such a table always goes into the methods or supplementary material.

count_files <- function(path) c(snp = length(readLines(paste0(path, ".bim"))),
                                ind = length(readLines(paste0(path, ".fam"))))

steps <- tribble(
  ~step,                                 ~command,                                ~file,
  "1 Biallelic SNPs (no indels)",        "`--snps-only just-acgt --max-alleles 2`", "eagle_0",
  "2 Individuals with ≤ 80% missing",    "`--mind 0.8`",                          "eagle_1_mind",
  "3 SNPs with ≤ 20% missing",           "`--geno 0.2`",                          "eagle_2_geno",
  "4 No duplicated samples",             "`--remove` (KING > 0.354)",             "eagle_3_no_duplicates",
  "5 MAF ≥ 0.05 (for Practical 5)",     "`--maf 0.05`",                          "eagle_4_maf05"
)

cascade <- steps |>
  mutate(n = map(file, \(f) count_files(r(f))),
         SNPs = map_int(n, "snp"),
         individuals = map_int(n, "ind")) |>
  select(-n)

bind_rows(tibble(step = "0 VCF (Dryad)", command = "", file = "eagle.vcf.gz",
                 SNPs = vcf_snp, individuals = length(columns) - 9L),
          cascade) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
               caption = "Filtering cascade: number of SNPs and individuals after each step.")
